lesson.title: Reading the Signal in Three Duplicate ACKs
lesson.summary: Fast retransmit lets TCP recover a lost segment almost immediately by treating three duplicate acknowledgments as strong evidence of loss, instead of waiting for a slow timeout.
lesson.body:
Recall that TCP acknowledgments are cumulative: an ACK for byte N tells the sender "I have received everything up through byte N minus one," regardless of what has arrived afterward. If a segment is lost but later segments in the same window arrive safely, the receiver cannot ACK past the gap. Every time another segment beyond the gap arrives, the receiver re-sends an ACK for the same byte number it already acknowledged, because that is still the last point of contiguous, in-order data it has. From the sender's point of view, these look like duplicate ACKs, several acknowledgments in a row for the same byte number.

A duplicate ACK is ambiguous by itself, since it could result from ordinary reordering in the network rather than genuine loss, so TCP does not react to just one or two of them. But when three duplicate ACKs arrive in a row (meaning four identical ACKs total: the original plus three duplicates), the pattern becomes strong evidence that a segment truly was lost and that the segments after it are still arriving safely. Fast retransmit reacts to this pattern immediately: rather than waiting for the retransmission timer to expire, which is deliberately conservative and can take a full round trip time or more to fire, the sender retransmits the missing segment as soon as the third duplicate ACK arrives.

This matters because the ordinary retransmission timeout, described in a later chapter, is set conservatively to avoid retransmitting segments that are simply delayed rather than lost. That conservatism is appropriate for actual timeouts, but it is far too slow for the common case of a single segment lost in an otherwise healthy, flowing connection. Duplicate ACKs give TCP a faster, more targeted signal: the receiver is actively telling the sender, "I am still getting your later data, just not this one piece," which is exactly the situation fast retransmit is built for.

Consider a sender transmitting segments 1 through 6 back to back. Segment 3 is lost in the network, but segments 4, 5, and 6 arrive at the receiver successfully. For segment 4, the receiver can only acknowledge through segment 2 (since segment 3 is still missing), so it sends a duplicate ACK requesting segment 3. The same happens for segment 5 and again for segment 6, producing three duplicate ACKs in a row, all requesting segment 3. Upon seeing the third duplicate ACK, the sender does not wait to see whether a fourth or fifth will arrive, and does not wait for its retransmission timer to expire. It immediately retransmits segment 3. This single change, reacting to duplicate ACKs instead of waiting on a timer, is one of the most effective early improvements to TCP's congestion control, because it turns what would have been a stall of one or more round trip times into a near-instant repair. What fast retransmit does not settle on its own is how the congestion window should respond to this loss event: that question is the subject of fast recovery, discussed next.
